item.title: My temporary PHP fix from 2014 has nearly 20M installs. Today I'm deprecating it
item.description:
Source: jakeasmith.com

Top Comment:

The announcement is the good outcome. Most of the rot I've been measuring this year never gets announced.

I've been autopsying frozen npm packages: load-grunt-config (no release since 2021), gulp-uglify (frozen since 2019-03), uglifyjs-webpack-plugin (741k installs/week, repo archived 2019-12, still not npm-deprecated), webpack-subresource-integrity (5.2M/week, and the npm "latest" tag has pointed at a release candidate since Feb 2023).

The pattern that actually bites isn't the abandoned repo. It's the frozen repo that still resolves. A wide range like uglify-js: ^3.0.5 doesn't ship the engine the package was tested against, it ships today's. gulp-uglify pinned nothing, and current uglify-js silently corrupts sloppy-mode param/arguments aliasing; the same corruption turns up in two packages I tested, both still installed hundreds of thousands of times a week.

So what jakeasmith is doing here does real work: it turns invisible rot into a visible migration. The genuinely dangerous case is the maintainer who goes quiet with no notice at all, where the only signals are a stale latest tag and an upstream bug a few major versions deep.

If anyone is checking their lockfile after reading this: pin the transitive engine, not just your direct dependency, and treat last-release date as a risk field. Install count tells you who is exposed, not whether it is maintained.

item.title: Reversing Factorio's RNG
item.description:
Source: gegell.github.io

Top Comment:

Stardew Valley has two random number seeds. One is the normal character seed. The other, your multiplayer ID, can be determined by analyzing the save file.

Except! On the Switch, you can't easily access the save file AND the random number generator is different than on PC. There is a seed cracker that looks at your traveling cart listing and calculates the character seed. Maybe because it's less important and harder to observe, I haven't found any tool to crack the other seed and don't have time to attempt writing it myself.

By inspecting cracked geode contents, you should be able to isolate your multiplayer ID and then predict random events on Nintendo just as PC players have done for the last decade with access to the save file.

The C# code for the game is online and the Switch RNG is known, so you never have to work in the dark. It's three steps: ensure your Switch RNG implementation works by testing against the normal seed, ensure your geode RNG implementation works by testing against the PC RNG, and then apply the Switch RNG to the geode function enough times that only one seed could create your observed sequence.

-----

Two semi-related open questions: Are you able to solve as quickly while starting at ANY geode as you'd be solving from the first geode? Does the RNG eventually repeat, so it actually doesn't matter what your multiplayer ID is as long as you observe a unique sequence, since there will only be one continuation of that sequence?

item.title: OpenSpec – A lightweight and configurable AI spec framework
item.description:
Source: openspec.dev

Top Comment:

I've used OpenSpec extensively on two large pieces of software which were worked solo over 6-9 months.

Recently, I've completely ditched the specification part. I found they just weren't useful over the longer term. I used an LLM to assess in both directions whether the code matched the specs and whether the specs matched the code. On both software projects this came out with huge divergence from spec to code.

Basically the old theory is true - the code IS the specification.

What I did find very useful and have retained is the process flow. Create a proposal, review the proposal, implement, review the code. Also useful was building and maintaining ADRs and invariant logs for where a unit test cannot be made to verify behaviour. The process and the ADRs, unit test, invariant log all help the software stay coherent as the LLM churns on it over many unconnected contexts.

item.title: Anecdotally, programmers dislike "reduce"
item.description:
Source: evanhahn.com

Top Comment:

Map and filter usually have only one arg and if they have 2, the 2nd is almost always a 0-based index. They look identical in most languages, even when Microsoft chooses to call them Select and Where.

Reduce has an accumulator and a 2-arg function and languages are not very consistent amongst each other as to whether it's reduce(initial_acc, callback(acc, elem)) or reduce(callback(acc, elem), initial_acc) or reduce(callback(elem, acc), initial_acc) or what.

Hard to remember. Also some languages have a version of reduce that doesn't take an initial accumulator at all, which is just a footgun waiting for you to hit an empty collection. Also ALSO, the accumulator can easily become awkward in languages that don't support anonymous types or don't support easy mutation of an anonymous type record. Which is most of them!
